content.comment_body: Hello everyone, I'm working on a program where I'd like to change internal memory states (for example, M1, M2, M3) to activate outputs such as Q1, Q2, Q3, using the TDE display. Is there a way to select which memory to change using keys like C1, C2, C3, and C4, then toggle the memory state with the enter key so outputs are triggered? I'm trying this on a test screen without physical inputs and would appreciate an example to build on.

Hello [user_name], I didn't quite understand why you need to use internal flags for switching outputs. You have the option to use cursor keys on your controller or TDE, and the F-keys on the TDE act similarly to digital input buttons in your program. You can find these functions under: Instructions > Constants > Digital. Remember to hold the ESC key before pressing your chosen cursor key, provided there's at least one active message text available. Softkeys can also be integrated into message texts and used for display switching by holding ESC for over 2 seconds. You can select softkeys and the ON function using cursor keys and confirm with OK or ENTER on the TDE.
As a reminder about using cursor keys: make sure at least one message text is present and currently active; hold the ESC key, then press the desired cursor key.
Your test program is set up correctly, but note that C3 and C4 only activate the outputs while the cursor keys are pressed.
I'm still not clear on why you're using flags here; the internal flags in [product_name] don't function like those in [product_name].
You can assign multiple functions to the F keys by linking their use to different conditions, such as which message text is active.

Depending on your setup, you can give the F-Keys multiple functions. Some approaches: 1) Use a hardware or software switch to toggle between normal and service mode, so F1-F4 perform different tasks (see attached example); 2) Use a counter so F1 increases and F2 decreases values, letting you select messages by counter value and assign F3/F4 to varied functions per message. Other variations exist, but I'll keep it brief.

I see your point. On my screens, F1 through F4 are already in use for other functions, leaving me with the arrow keys, which I'd like to use as F keys. In your example, I couldn't activate output Q2—only Q1 responded. If I can figure out how this mechanism works, it might be what I need.
Testing the program on my [product_name] worked as expected; the second softkey toggled output Q2 on and off.

Does your test program function on both the actual device and the simulator? When I ran it in the simulator, only Q1 responded. I haven’t yet tested it on the actual hardware since I’m away, but I will check tomorrow.

Thank you. I considered a similar approach but am encountering difficulties because all inputs are already in use, including the F keys. Only the C keys remain, and I'm unsure how to apply them. In the simulator, the C keys work, but after downloading the program to the device, it doesn’t function. Any ideas on what might be going wrong?
I've included a screen recording of the simulation to help clarify.

If you review my previous reply and the provided example, you can address your issue by adding AND blocks to differentiate between normal and service modes. This would require some changes to your existing program, but it’s straightforward. I'd recommend using cursor keys only if other options aren't available. There are multiple menu-building examples using F-keys when you have a TDE display. If you share more about your programming approach, you'll get even more detailed support.

Reviewing my earlier message and the example, you can solve this by adding AND blocks for mode switching. Changing your existing program is necessary, but it’s simple. Use cursor keys only if you have no other way. There are many examples for menu creation with F-keys if TDE display is present. Providing more details on your setup will help others offer better guidance. I appreciate your patience and the help I've received. I’ve grasped the concept and plan to try it soon. Out of curiosity: If I use cursor keys like function keys on the TDE to trigger an output—say, pressing the up arrow to activate Q1—how would that implementation work?

See the attached screen recording. I now understand how to use the functions. I plan to test on both device and TDE Display at home and will share updates tomorrow. Thank you for your assistance so far—I’ll report back soon.

Let me repeat: 1) Make sure at least one message text exists and is active. 2) Hold the ESC key first, then press the desired cursor key. When simulating, only the cursor key needs to be pressed, but on real hardware you must first hold ESC, then the cursor key.
All is clear now. I didn’t realize that’s how it worked. I will test on the actual device tomorrow and follow up. Thanks in advance.

[user_name] and [user_name], hi! Just letting you know I tested the suggestions and set up the program using both function keys and Up/Down keys with softkey selection when needed. I was hoping for a simpler approach, but with your help, I managed to create something functional. Thanks to everyone for your advice. One more question: What do the 'protections active' and 'show message information in details' options do in the LOGO TDE configuration screen?
1) 'Protection Active': When enabled, parameters that can be changed via the display are locked and can only be viewed, not edited. 2) 'Show message information in details': See attached example.
Thanks for your assistance, and please excuse my English—I'm still learning.
Thank you once again to everyone for your support and assistance in resolving my issue.
Hello [user_name], you're most welcome ...

analysis.insight_summary: The user is facing challenges programming interaction between operator keys on the display and internal memory flags to control outputs without using physical inputs. There's confusion over the differences between internal flags in various programming environments and uncertainty about softkey, F-key, and cursor key integration for output control. Discussions highlight the complexity of multi-assigning keys, as well as differing behaviors between simulation and on actual hardware.
analysis.user_expectations: The user hopes to directly control internal memory and outputs via specific display keys (such as cursor arrows), without relying on physical digital inputs. They expect programming to work consistently between simulation and actual hardware and seek clear guidance for multi-functional key setups.
